title: Asynchronous KV Tiering & Adaptive Batching Deep Dive with Nova Ventures
summary: Deep technical session covering asynchronous KV tiering design, multi-layer KV cache eviction/eviction policies, adaptive batching heuristics for variable-length user prompts (128k+), quantization trade-offs for latency vs. quality, and private deployment (VPC / on-prem) constraints. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot with benchmark harness and share security docs and runbook.
topics: asynchronous KV tiering architecture (RAM -> NVMe -> remote)
adaptive batching heuristics for throughput/latency SLOs
KV eviction strategies for long-context (128k+) workloads
quantization impacts on perplexity and hallucination rates
networking / VPC peering and cold-starts in on-prem deployments
benchmark plan and success criteria for pilot
action_items: Jordan Lee - Share benchmark harness spreadsheet, pilot runbook, and sample prompt set - due 2027-01-05
Priya Nambiar - Provision a small Dedicated test pool config and provide initial perf knobs - due 2026-12-28
Devon Clarke (Nova) - Supply representative long-form prompt logs and storage profile (percent of append vs random access) - due 2026-12-29
Marcus Holt - Produce a short doc on asynchronous KV tiering internals (eviction, reclamation, hot-key detection) - due 2027-01-03
next_steps: Run a 2-week pilot with 128k prompt replay using Redwood Dedicated config (initial: 4xA100 equivalent)
Share SOC2/ISO appendices and on-prem network checklist
Schedule bench-run start next Tues (2026-12-28) and sync cadence weekly
Deliver preliminary perf report after first 48h of pilot
transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-12-21
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood SE), Marcus Holt (Redwood Solutions Eng), Elliot James (Nova CTO), Marina Soto (Nova ML Eng), Devon Clarke (Nova Infra), Sasha Kim (Nova Product)

Summary section (auto): Short recap at top — team wants to validate 128k+ context perf with near-production traffic shape; main concerns are tail latencies when cold KV pages are demanded, and quality regression due to quantization when using nvme-backed KV tiers.

00:00 Jordan Lee: hey everyone, thanks for making time today, um we've been looking forward to walking through the asynchronous kv tiering idea and how adaptive batching ties into it, we've got Priya and Marcus on to cover perf knobs
00:18 Elliot James: yeah thanks, Jordan. quick context, we've got a user-persona that uploads multi-doc legal files, average session lengths go way beyond 128k tokens in a single thread, sometimes they append iteratively which creates a very append-heavy workload — sorry, append heavy — and we care a lot about 95th and 99th pct latencies
00:42 Priya Nambiar: got it, that append versus random access profile really changes the eviction strategy, append-heavy means you can get away with streaming-optimized prefetch and more aggressive KV compaction otherwise you end up thrashing the nvme layer
01:03 Marina Soto: can you just define nvme layer again — like is this the local-instance SSD on the node or remote disk? we saw mention of both in the docs
01:12 Marcus Holt: yeah quick clarification — in the architecture we're proposing a three tier kv: RAM (hot), local NVMe (warm), and remote object store or remote KV for cold. Asynchronous tiering means background IO moves data between tiers without blocking token generation when possible
01:34 Devon Clarke: right but that background IO still adds jitter because if the KV miss happens during generation you sometimes have a sync path, right?
01:43 Priya Nambiar: correct, there is a sync fallback. we try to hide most misses by prefetch heuristics and hot-key tracking but cold misses can still trigger a synchronous fetch. the goal of asynchronous reclamation is to keep the hot set large enough to avoid those common misses while using nvme for the less frequently hit context
02:02 Elliot James: what about eviction criteria — lru works poorly for winds of continuous appends, we saw that in our prod traces, lru chased the tail and performance tanked
02:15 Jordan Lee: good point, Priya, can you talk about weighted recency + size aware eviction?
02:20 Priya Nambiar: sure, we use a hybrid TTL + adaptive recency where append streams gain a temporary "affinity" tag so recent appends are less likely to be evicted for a short window, then size aware cost function evicts large KV blobs that are cold to keep RAM density high
02:42 Marina Soto: hmm affinity tag — do you persist that to the nvme or only in memory?
02:47 Marcus Holt: affinity metadata is persisted to nvme as lightweight markers, so across restarts the scoring still prefers those keys for warm caching; we avoid full in-memory indices otherwise RAM overhead explodes for 128k contexts
03:05 Sasha Kim: question, is there a risk that persisting metadata becomes a new write amplification problem on nvme?
03:12 Priya Nambiar: we batch metadata writes and use append-friendly WAL segments, so we aim for sequential writes; still a hardware endurance consideration though — we'll include an endurance budget in the runbook
03:30 Jordan Lee: switching to batching — Marcus, can you outline the adaptive batching heuristic we demoed in the lab?
03:38 Marcus Holt: yes. so, adaptive batching watches request size distribution and target SLOs and does a dynamic tradeoff: for small requests we batch aggressively up to Xms or up to a token-count ceiling, for very long-context requests (128k+) we prefer a streaming path with micro-batches to keep latency reasonable. there are feedback loops: if GPU utilization drops below threshold we increase batch size, if tail latency increases we shrink it
04:05 Devon Clarke: what's the control loop period? every 10s? 30s? we worry about oscillation in autoscaling land
04:13 Marcus Holt: default is 30s with smoothing; production customers often set 60s for stability. the heuristic uses EWMA over request size and latency percentiles to avoid rapid oscillations
04:30 Marina Soto: for our workload, many requests are variable — sometimes a long 120k append, sometimes short queries embedded — does adaptive batching slow down the shorts while waiting for micro batch windows?
04:45 Priya Nambiar: micro-batch windows are prioritized heuristically: we ensure a small-request fast-path that bypasses batch waiting if it's latency sensitive based on a QoS flag, but if you mark everything latency sensitive you lose batching gains, so we recommend per-route QoS config
05:10 Elliot James: can we see numbers? what are you seeing for token/sec and 95/99 latency for a 4xA100 equivalent config under a mixed traffic replay?
05:25 Marcus Holt: in our internal lab with mixed replay (70% short, 30% long append), 4xA100 equiv showed sustained 480k tokens/sec, median token latency ~6ms, 95th around 220ms, 99th spikes around 850ms when synchronous cold fetches occur — with nvme warm tier these 99th spikes drop to ~320ms after the hot set stabilizes
06:00 Marina Soto: that's helpful, do those numbers account for quantized kernels? like int8 or q4_0?
06:10 Priya Nambiar: the lab runs were using q4_0 kernels; full fp16 runs lower latency but higher cost. quantization introduced a small quality delta — around 1.7% relative increase in perplexity on our eval prompt set — sometimes more noticeable on code-generation style prompts
06:30 Elliot James: so quantization is maybe ok for customer-facing summarization but not for our legal-code extraction pipelines, right? we need to be careful about hallucination regressions
06:42 Priya Nambiar: exactly. we recommend a hybrid approach: keep critical model paths fp16 or higher precision, use quantized variants for bulk summarization and embeddings where quality demands are lower. Redwood's runtime can hot-swap model variants per-route for that reason
07:05 Devon Clarke: on private deployment, what's the network topology for remote cold-tier? do you offer a private object store connector inside VPC or do we have to host the cold tier ourselves?
07:16 Jordan Lee: for Redwood Private we support VPC peering and an optional object-store bridge; customers can host cold-tier in their cloud region or on-prem object store. we provide an S3-like connector and an encrypted transfer path with chunked uploads
07:34 Marina Soto: any requirements for bandwidth? if our remote cold-tier is in a different region will that blow up latency for misses?
07:42 Marcus Holt: yes cross-region misses are costly. we recommend colocating warm nvme tier in the same AZ as compute. remote cold-tier is meant for deep cold objects; we prefetch using hinting to reduce cross-region fetches. bandwidth sizing depends on your miss rate, we'll provide a calculator in the runbook
08:05 Sasha Kim: about metrics, can we get token-level tracing to map user session IDs to KV hits/misses? we want to understand per-customer tail behavior
08:15 Priya Nambiar: yes, Redwood Console supports per-request tracing and token-level hit/miss logs, you can filter by session id. note though that high-cardinality tracing adds overhead; we sample at 1% by default but can increase for short windows during the pilot
08:34 Elliot James: any security gotchas with persisting affinity metadata? encryption at rest and KMS?
08:40 Jordan Lee: all persisted metadata and KV blobs are encrypted at rest; for Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM. we also provide audit logs and RBAC so you can control who reads the traces
08:56 Marina Soto: quick aside, how do you handle cold-start when a large model variant is pulled into GPU memory for the first time? we saw some jitter from warmup kernels
09:06 Marcus Holt: model load is parallelized but still takes time; we avoid repeated loads by keeping a small LRU of model shards in memory and pre-warming common variants. also quantized kernels sometimes allow faster cold loads due to smaller memory footprint
09:23 Devon Clarke: if we want deterministic latency for SLAs, is there a recommended fallback — always use a smaller fp16 model to guarantee latency?
09:31 Priya Nambiar: yes you can define pinned model fallback policies per route: if the high-capacity variant is unavailable or load spikes, route to a smaller fp16 that maintains latency SLOs. Redwood supports canary and automatic fallback configs
09:46 Elliot James: ok, about the pilot: what instrumentation do you recommend we include from our side? disk metrics, io wait, network RTTs?
09:54 Marcus Holt: yes: NVMe latency histograms, queue depth, OS-level io_wait, GPU util, PCIe link saturations, and token-level hit/miss logs. also we want a sample of your prompt distributions with anonymized metadata (no PII)
10:16 Marina Soto: i'll flag with legal about logs, but we can anonymize. Devon will send infra metrics.
10:25 Devon Clarke: quick thing — our compliance team will want to run an encryption and SOC2 mapping review before we put any PII in logs
10:33 Jordan Lee: understood; we'll share the SOC2 appendix and the on-prem checklist after this call
10:42 Sasha Kim: more on adaptive batching — can the runtime bias the batching to favor requests from certain customers (like enterprise customers) to protect their SLO?
10:51 Priya Nambiar: yes per-tenant QoS and weighted batching is supported; we maintain per-tenant rate-limit and QoS buckets so enterprise customers can be prioritized in the scheduler
11:06 Elliot James: curious — you mentioned hot-key detection, how do you detect a 'hot' key in an append stream vs repeated reads?
11:14 Marcus Holt: we maintain a sliding-window frequency sketch and a recency counter; append streams get an affinity boost but reads that show repeated hits rapidly increase frequency score. we then use a small top-k heap to track candidates for RAM promotion
11:34 Marina Soto: any risk of sketch poisoning or adversarial patterns? if a user floods with fake hits to push others out?
11:42 Priya Nambiar: a good question — we have rate limiting and a write-amplification guard, plus we decay scores for suspicious traffic patterns. we'll advise on anomaly detection thresholds in the runbook
12:00 Jordan Lee: ok jumping to quantization details — what quant kernels do you support and what are the observed tradeoffs?
12:09 Priya Nambiar: supported kernels include q4_0, q4_1, int8 dynamic, and fp16. q4_0 has the smallest footprint but slightly higher quality delta; q4_1 balances quality and latency. int8 dynamic is promising for some transformer variants but needs per-model calibration
12:27 Marina Soto: do you provide a per-prompt eval harness to measure hallucination regressions? we need to know not just perplexity but downstream extraction accuracy
12:37 Marcus Holt: yes we can run your prompt set through the harness and supply EVAL metrics including extraction F1, hallucination rate, and a side-by-side diff between model variants
12:50 Elliot James: nice. what's the expected timeline to get that back?
12:54 Jordan Lee: we can turn a baseline report in 48-72 hours after we get prompts and a target list from you
13:10 Sasha Kim: will the bench include cold-miss stress tests — like artificially forcing eviction and replaying long-context misses to measure 99/99.9?
13:18 Priya Nambiar: yes that's part of the pilot stress plan, we have scripts to evict hot set and replay at various rates to measure tail behavior
13:33 Devon Clarke: any storage recommendations — like using enterprise-grade NVMe with higher TBW?
13:40 Marcus Holt: yes we suggest enterprise NVMe for the warm tier; consumer drives show endurance issues under constant write-heavy append profiles. we'll include a hardware shortlist in the runbook
13:55 Elliot James: okay — can we talk about cost? if we keep a large warm set in NVMe and big RAM footprint, costs balloon; how do you recommend balancing that?
14:06 Jordan Lee: the Optimize toolkit helps: it recommends quantization per route, sets batching targets, and suggests warm-tier sizing based on hit-rate targets. for pilots we aim for a working set that keeps miss rate under a threshold to make cost predictable
14:26 Marina Soto: what's a reasonable warm set ratio for our append-heavy profile to get 99th latency under 500ms?
14:33 Marcus Holt: ballpark: aim for warm set to cover 65-75% of active working set for append-heavy traces; exact number depends on average KV blob sizes — we'll compute in the calculator
14:50 Sasha Kim: do you have any case studies where this architecture saved costs compared to purely in-RAM serving?
14:58 Jordan Lee: yes, a media customer moved 40% of their cold context to NVMe and cut monthly infra cost ~32% while keeping 95th latency within SLOs — we'll anonymize and share that case study with the pilot materials
15:15 Elliot James: good. last quick thing — competitor question: does CumulusAI offer similar asynchronous tiering?
15:22 Priya Nambiar: public materials from CumulusAI talk about multi-tier caching but they don't show persistent affinity metadata or per-route hot-swap model variants. EdgeServe focuses more on on-prem orchestration but less on dynamic batching heuristics
15:40 Jordan Lee: ok thanks all, let's summarize next steps — Jordan to share bench spreadsheet and SOC2 appendix; Priya/Marcus to prepare pilot config and runbook; Nova to share prompt logs and infra metrics; scheduled bench start 2026-12-28
15:58 Elliot James: sounds good. thanks everyone!
16:03 Jordan Lee: thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invite for the pilot kickoff and the documents
